title: Two-level review flow: four-eyes state machine
scenario: Replay claim/pass/request_changes/reject/resubmit events through a two-level review state machine with conflict-of-interest rules, then report history, the waiting queue (higher priority first), reviewer stats and cycle times. Test 3 is the summary.

verified.why_correct: It tries exactly the three formats in the README, month/day for the slash form, and raises on anything else rather than guessing.
Authors can never claim, and the level-1 reviewer is only blocked at level 2. Both raise ConflictOfInterest, which is a subclass of AssignmentError, so the handler has to catch it first.

bugs.title: Broad except clause catches conflicts first
bugs.symptom: Test 1 test_rejection_reasons: the three conflict_of_interest entries (rae on T1, cho on T3, eli on T8) show 'not_assignee'. The refused events themselves are right.
bugs.why: ConflictOfInterest subclasses AssignmentError, and Python uses the first except clause that matches. With the parent clause first, every conflict is labelled not_assignee and the conflict branch can never run.
hints: The right events are refused, only the reason is off. Which exception does a conflict raise?
Look at the class hierarchy in models.py and the order of the except clauses in handle().
probes: Why are the other reasons (unknown_task, invalid_transition) unaffected?
How could the hierarchy be designed so the clause order matters less?

bugs.title: History list shared by every task
bugs.old:
decided_at = None

    def __init__(self, task_id, author, priority, submitted_at):
        self.task_id = task_id
        self.author = author
        self.priority = priority
        self.submitted_at = submitted_at
        self.entered_at = submitted_at
        self.history = []
bugs.new:
decided_at = None
    history = []

    def __init__(self, task_id, author, priority, submitted_at):
        self.task_id = task_id
        self.author = author
        self.priority = priority
        self.submitted_at = submitted_at
        self.entered_at = submitted_at
bugs.symptom: Test 2 test_history: T1's history is one long list beginning 'submitted', 'submitted', 'submitted', ... (88 entries in a full run) instead of 5 states. Every task returns that same list.
bugs.why: `history = []` on the class is a single list. append() mutates it through every instance, unlike `self.state = ...`, which creates a per-instance attribute. So all tasks share one ever-growing history.
hints: Every task's history is the same long list. Where does each task get its list?
Look at the class-level attributes on Task and which of them are mutated rather than reassigned.
Create the list per instance: self.history = [] in __init__ (and drop the class attribute).
probes: Why are state, revision and l1_reviewer safe as class-level defaults when history isn't?
Why didn't states or cycle times change?

bugs.title: reverse=True also reverses the tie-breaks
bugs.symptom: Test 2 test_waiting_queue: the priority-2 tasks come out T7, T12, T11 instead of T11, T12, T7. T2 is still first and T10 still last.
bugs.why: reverse=True flips the whole key, so among equal priorities the most recently queued task comes first instead of the one that has waited longest.
hints: T2 and T10 are in the right places. Look at the three priority-2 tasks.
Check the sort key and direction in waiting_queue against the README's queue rule.
Negate priority and drop reverse=True: key=lambda t: (-t.priority, t.entered_at, t.task_id).
probes: Why does negating just the priority fix it?
Why should T7 (submitted earliest) come after T11 and T12?

bugs.title: Actor names only trimmed
bugs.symptom: Test 2 test_reviewer_stats: the table has both 'Dana' {passed 1, changes 1} and 'dana' {passed 1} instead of one 'dana' {passed 2, changes 1}.
bugs.why: Authors are lower-cased but actors are only trimmed, so 'Dana' and 'dana' count as two reviewers. Each spelling is used consistently within a task, so the state machine still works and only the stats split.
hints: There's a 'Dana' and a 'dana' in the reviewer table. Should there be?
Compare how people are normalised in load_tasks and load_events.
probes: Which data would turn this into a real security problem for the four-eyes rule?
Why did the state machine still accept all of Dana's actions on T3?

bugs.title: timedelta.seconds drops whole days
bugs.symptom: Test 3 test_cycle_hours: T3 is 0.5 instead of 24.5. Every other task matches.
bugs.why: `timedelta.seconds` is only the seconds part after removing whole days (0–86399). T3's 24.5 hours becomes 0.5.
hints: Only T3 is off, and it's the only cycle longer than a day.
Look at how elapsed time is turned into hours in metrics.py.
probes: What are timedelta's three stored components?
Why did T8 (23.7 h) still come out right?

bugs.title: Enum state compared to a string
bugs.old: approved = sum(1 for t in tasks if t.state is State.APPROVED)
bugs.new: approved = sum(1 for t in tasks if t.state == "approved")
bugs.symptom: Test 3 test_approval_rate: `0.0 != 0.571`. by_state still shows 4 approved.
bugs.why: State is a plain Enum, so State.APPROVED == 'approved' is False. No task counts as approved and the rate becomes 0.0, while by_state (which uses .value) is still right.
hints: by_state says 4 approved, yet approval_rate is 0.0.
Compare how by_state and approved read the state in summarize().
probes: Would making State subclass str change this? What are the trade-offs?
Why didn't the rejected count have the same problem?

context_qa.q: How does build_report run the replay?
context_qa.a: It loads tasks.csv into Task objects, builds a ReviewMachine, calls `machine.handle(event)` for every event in file order, and then builds each report section from the machine's tasks (sorted by task number), `accepted` events and `rejected` (event, reason) pairs.

context_qa.q: What does ReviewMachine.apply do with an event?
context_qa.a: It looks up the task (UnknownTask if missing), finds a method named `_<action>` (InvalidTransition if there is none), calls it, and appends the event to `accepted` if nothing raised. handle() wraps apply() and maps the raised exception class to a reason string.

context_qa.q: What exception classes exist and how are they related?
context_qa.a: In models.py: ReviewError is the base; UnknownTask, InvalidTransition and AssignmentError subclass it; ConflictOfInterest subclasses AssignmentError.

context_qa.q: Where is a task's history recorded?
context_qa.a: Task.__init__ starts it with State.SUBMITTED, and Task.move appends each new state (and also sets state, entered_at, and decided_at for approved/rejected). The report converts each entry with `.value`.

context_qa.q: Which timestamp does the waiting queue use?
context_qa.a: `entered_at`, which Task.move updates on every transition. A resubmitted task's entered_at is therefore its resubmit time, not its original submitted_at.
reviewer_stats walks the accepted events: a `claim` makes sure the actor has an entry, and pass/request_changes/reject increment passed/changes/rejected for that actor. Resubmits aren't counted.
For tasks whose state is in DECIDED, the difference decided_at − submitted_at (both datetimes) converted to hours and rounded to 1 decimal.
